author: Deanne King
title: Tampa Bay native Olympian combats racial disparities in drowning deaths through swim lessons - NewsBreak
text:
By Deanne King ,
14 hours ago
TAMPA, Fla. (WFLA) — Maritza McClendon broke racial barriers as the first Afro-Latina woman to make it onto the U.S. Olympic Swimming Team, and now she is ensuring the same opportunity is afforded to minority children across the country.
Born in Puerto Rico, but raised in Brandon, Fl, Maritza McClendon didn’t know how to swim until a scolosis diagnosis changed her life at 6-years-old.
Sigma Gamma Rho brings service, multi-million dollar impact to Tampa “Doctors said I’m probably going to have to have surgery,” McClendon recalled. “My mom said absolutely not what other options do we have and the doctor recommended swimming to my mom and she said okay let’s go ahead and try it.”
At six, McClendon didn’t know how to swim, so her physical therapy started with her learning water safety and the swim basics. After learning the ropes, her instructor introduced her to the sport of swimming. Not only did swimming cure her scoliosis, but six years later she started winning major competitions across the Tampa Bay area and beating kids twice her age.
McClendon went on to earn a full ride swimming scholarship to the University of Georgia. There she won 11 NCAA titles and is a 27 time All American. In 2000, she went out for the U.S. Olympic Team but didn’t make it. After overcoming the devastation, she went out for the Olympic Team again in 2004. Well, that time she made it and then went on to win the silver medal in the 4x100m freestyle relay. She made history as the first Black woman to ever do so.
It’s a journey many kids who look like her don’t get. According to the CDC, Black children are nearly three times more likely to die while swimming in a pool. McClendon now spends her time hosting swim clinics, teaching water safety and swim lessons across minority community to combat those racial disparities.
“When I started swimming I was in Puerto Rico,” she said. “There were a lot of kids and families that looked just like me and mine. It felt like home. I moved to Tampa, walked on the pool deck with a team of 150 kids and me, my brother and two other families were the only Black families a part of that team. Unfortunately, 64% of Black kids don’t know how to swim, 40% of Hispanic kids don’t know how to swim and 1 in 3 Black adults say they have never had formal swim lessons. Drowning statistics plague our communities higher than any other community out there, so this is the work I absolutely love to do.”
McClendon hosts swim clinics across the country and even comes back home to Tampa Bay to conduct them as well. Be sure to follow her on social media and check out her website for her upcoming clinics.
